newsitem.title: USA: Greenspan seen guardedly optimistic on U.S. economy.
newsitem.headline: Greenspan seen guardedly optimistic on U.S. economy.

text.p: Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan is expected to describe the U.S. economy in upbeat terms when he testifies to lawmakers this week, emphasising its stable growth and surprisingly low inflation.
But his testimony is also likely to include some words of caution about the course of inflation and possibly the stock market.

"Greenspan will take a measured tone," said Gary Schlossberg, chief economist at Wells Fargo Bank. "He will probably voice satisfaction with the inflation data of late and with recent numbers showing the economy settling back to a sustainable pace."

Still, economists expect Greenspan to echo his previous public remarks and those of other Fed officials about the possibility that rising wages, due to tight U.S. labour markets, could eventually lead to higher inflation.

While Greenspan will leave open the possibility of an interest-rate rise to head off a potential pickup in inflation, analysts said his remarks will not contain any suggestions of an imminent rate move.

"The statements coming from Fed officials have indicated that if they feel they need to raise interest rates they will do so, but perhaps not necessarily right now," said Joel Prakken of the consulting firm Macroeconomic Advisers LLC.
Greenspan is to testify before the Senate Banking Committee at 1500 GMT on Wednesday and before a House Banking subcommittee on March 5.
The Fed chief's twice yearly report to Congress on the economy and monetary policy, called for under a law known as Humphrey-Hawkins, is watched closely by financial markets.
The report comes with the unemployment rate at 5.4 percent and underlying inflation hovering near 30-year lows.
While economists have been concerned about the inflation risks posed by the low unemployment rate, signs that the economy has slowed after a boom at the end of last year have eased some fears.
"The labour market is really the only precursor of inflation that is flashing red right now," said Roger Brinner, executive director at DRI/McGraw Hill, an economic consultant.
With the unemployment rate below the 5.5 percent to 6 percent range associated with higher inflation in the past, economists and many Fed officials have expressed surprise at benign price data.

Greenspan will offer some reasons in his formal testimony for the favourable inflation performance and perhaps an explanation as to why the Fed has opted to leave interest rates steady for the time being, Brinner said.
In addition to listening for hints on the direction of interest rates, financial market traders will be attuned to any remarks from the Fed Chairman about the stock market.
Greenspan roiled world financial markets in December when he used the phrase "irrational exuberance" in describing the markets.
Minutes from meetings of the central bank's policy-makers in recent months have suggested they are monitoring the nation's stock market, which has enjoyed a huge run-up.
However, Greenspan was expected to approach the subject of the stock market gingerly and may not even mention it explicitly in his formal remarks to Congress.

"In light of the reaction in December, Greenspan will have some carefully selected remarks if the subject comes up during the question-and-answer session," said former Fed governor Lyle Gramley, now a consulting economist at the Mortgage Bankers Association.
"Given the interest in it, it is sure to come up."
